Before a language model works with text, a tokeniser breaks it into reusable pieces and represents them as numbers. A piece might be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation or a single character. The exact split depends on the tokeniser.
That is why a limit of 10,000 tokens does not mean 10,000 words. The document, instructions and conversation can all take up space, and the system also needs room to produce its answer.

If a document is too large for a task, shorten irrelevant material or work on clearly labelled sections. Keep the passages needed to interpret each section together. Cutting a policy into pieces is not helpful if the exception ends up separated from the rule.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: 4.2 — What a Token Actually Is 📼 Rewind it: If you ever cut words and letters from magazines for a school-project title, you already know the basic move: build new text from a fixed box of reusable pieces. A tokeniser also works with reusable pieces — but its pieces may be a whole word, part of one, punctuation, or one character. It is not reading the pieces or deciding what they mean. The intuition is simple: a token is a word. One word = one token. That's close, but wrong in ways that matter. A token is a chunk — sometimes a whole word, sometimes part of a word, sometimes just a single character or a punctuation mark. The system has a fixed vocabulary of these chunks (typically 50,000–100,000 of them), and every piece of text you give it gets broken into pieces from that vocabulary. Real examples: The sentence "I love playing basketball" might get split like this: Text Tokens I I love love playing play + ing basketball basket + ball "Love" is common enough to be one token. "Playing" gets split into "play" and "ing" — because "ing" appears at the end of thousands of words, so the system learned to treat it as its own chunk. "Basketball" splits into "basket" + "ball" — two familiar pieces. Now a less common word: "tokenisation" might split into token + isation — or even token + is + ation , depending on the specific system. And something unusual — a rare word, a name, a technical term the system hasn't seen often — gets chopped into smaller and smaller pieces, sometimes all the way down to individual letters. The rule of thumb: In English, one token is roughly three-quarters of a word. So 100 words ≈ 130 tokens. A full page of text is about 500–700 tokens. 💡 Why not just use whole words? Because there are too many of them. English alone has hundreds of thousands of words, plus names, technical terms, slang, new words being invented constantly. You'd need an infinitely large vocabulary. By splitting into subword chunks, the system can handle any word it's never seen before — it just breaks it into smaller familiar pieces. It's a balance between efficiency (common words stay whole) and flexibility (rare words get broken down). Think of it like Scrabble tiles — but instead of individual letters, you have tiles for common chunks: one tile for "the", one for "ing", one for "un", one for "tion". Common words are just one tile.
